questions.q: In this capstone's framing, how do Chapters 1-7 map onto the prevention, detection, and response layers of a security program?
options: Chapters 1 and 6 are prevention, Chapters 2, 3, 5, and 7 are detection, and Chapter 4 is response
Every chapter is purely a detection technique with no prevention or response component at all
Only Chapter 4 matters; the other seven chapters are optional background material
Prevention, detection, and response are unrelated to how this course was structured
questions.explain: Firewalls and vulnerability scanning keep problems out before detection has to catch anything; IDS/IPS, traffic analysis, threat intel, and deception catch what prevention missed; EDR response is what happens once something is caught.

questions.q: Why didn't Chapter 1's firewall rules alone stop the exfiltration in Lesson 31's case study?
options: The exfiltration traffic looked like ordinary outbound HTTPS, which firewall rules are not designed to distinguish from legitimate traffic by appearance alone
The firewall in that case study was misconfigured and allowed all traffic by mistake
Firewalls were never covered in this course
The exfiltration happened entirely inside the DMZ, where no firewall rules apply
questions.explain: The traffic's outbound HTTPS appearance required flow baselining, threat intel, and EDR telemetry together — layers beyond what firewall rules alone could catch.

questions.q: Which chapter's concepts supplied the second signal (the threat-intel-flagged destination IP) in Lesson 31's case study?
options: Chapter 5 — Threat Intelligence & Indicators of Compromise
Chapter 6 — Vulnerability Assessment & Scanning
Chapter 1 — Firewall Architecture & Network Segmentation
Chapter 7 — Honeypots & Deception Technology
questions.explain: Chapter 5 covered IOCs and threat intelligence feeds, which is exactly what flagged the destination IP in Lesson 31's exfiltration case.

questions.q: Why are honeypot alerts from Chapter 7 described as unusually high-fidelity compared to most other detection sources?
options: Because no legitimate user ever has a reason to interact with a honeypot, so any interaction is inherently suspicious
Because honeypots require no configuration or maintenance once deployed
Because honeypots can only be deployed on networks with no other security controls
Because honeypot alerts are generated automatically by vulnerability scanners
questions.explain: A honeypot has no legitimate business purpose, so unlike a firewall or IDS alert, nearly every interaction with one is a genuine signal rather than normal traffic that needs filtering out.

questions.q: What course comes next in this career path after Network Security, Endpoint Protection & Threat Detection is complete?
options: SOC Operations, SIEM & Log Analysis
Windows, Linux & Security Administration
There is no further course in this path
Advanced Databricks & Delta Lake
questions.explain: This lesson's outro names SOC Operations, SIEM & Log Analysis as the next course in the Cybersecurity Analyst to Security Engineer path.
